title: I have chosen once
hookLine: Narada praises the young man Savitri has chosen, then names his one flaw: he will die within a year
carry: satya: mind, word and deed as one

cards: Savitri has just said his name, and the sage Narada says: oh no. He doesn't mean the young man is bad. Quite the opposite.
Ashvapati asks what's wrong with Satyavan, and Narada starts listing what's right. He's truthful. He's generous.
He's patient, handsome, kind to everyone. Every good thing you could want. And then the sage stops, and says there's one flaw, and it outweighs all the rest.

teach.b: The flaw is this, Narada says: a year from today, Satyavan will die. The court goes quiet. Her father turns to Savitri at once: go, choose someone else.
And Savitri answers, in the telling, something like this. Some things happen only once. A daughter is given in marriage once.
I have chosen once. Whether his life is long or short, I have chosen my husband, and I won't choose twice. My mind decided first, then my words said it, and now I'll act on it.
That last line is the teaching. Hindus have a three-word phrase for it: manasa, vacha, karmana. In mind, in word, in deed.
When the three agree, that's satya, truth, one of the deepest values in Hindu dharma. Satya isn't only not lying.

teach.h: SATYA: ONE PERSON ALL THE WAY THROUGH.
teach.b: It's being one person all the way through. Many Hindus end their daily prayers with a verse that offers to God everything done by body, by speech and by mind.
And notice the man she chose: Satyavan, whose very name means the truthful one. Narada doesn't argue. Her mind is steady, he tells the king; let it be.
He blesses the marriage and goes.
Ashvapati travels into the forest to find old blind Dyumatsena, who worries: we live on what the forest gives; how could a princess bear it? She knows all of it, Ashvapati says.
The two fathers agree, and Savitri marries Satyavan among the hermitages, carrying news her husband doesn't know. For today: satya isn't proved when a promise is easy.
It's proved when the news turns bad, and your mind, your words and your actions still line up.

how: In the Mahabharata's telling, Narada's warning and Savitri's reply, that her mind decided, her words said it and she will act on it, both come before the wedding; Hindus name that agreement of mind, word and deed as satya.

o: the sage who brings bad news to the royal court
the blind king who lost his kingdom to an enemy
the truthful son with one year left, chosen anyway

p: asks if a princess can bear the forest

s: satya, in Hindu teaching, only means not telling lies
it's mind, word and deed agreeing: Savitri decided, said it, and acted on it.
Savitri's father urged her to choose someone else
Ashvapati asked her to choose again, and she refused.
Savitri married Satyavan without knowing the warning
she heard Narada's warning and married him knowing it.

games.q: you told your cousin you'd help at her sangeet on saturday. then friends invite you somewhere better. by Savitri's satya, what fits?
o: go with your friends; you never wrote it down.
keep it: you decided, you said it, now do it.
show up for ten minutes and slip out.
games.why: manasa, vacha, karmana: mind, word and deed. Savitri chose once and acted on it, even when the news turned bad.

practice: Many Hindus close their prayers by offering whatever they've done in body, speech and mind. Bring to mind one promise you've made. On the breath in, check your mind: do I still mean it?

On the breath out, check your words and your actions: do they match it? If you pray, offer all three, mind, word and deed; if not, simply notice where they line up and where they don't, without scolding yourself.

wordCard.voice: Satyavan. His name means the truthful one, and the bride who chose him keeps her word in mind, in speech and in act.

orig.note: Sanskrit Satyavan, 'the truthful one', the son of Dyumatsena whom Narada praises.

carryVoice: Your line: satya: mind, word and deed as one. Savitri chose once, and stayed chosen. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Pativrata-mahatmya: Narada's praise of Satyavan and his warning; Ashvapati's plea; Savitri's reply; Narada's blessing; Ashvapati visits Dyumatsena; the marriage)
Bhagavata Purana 11.2.36 (kayena vacha manasa...: offering to Narayana all that is done by body, speech and mind; widely recited at the close of puja)
